title: Daily Health Briefing
intro: Good morning! Today's digest leans into fresh 2026 human trials and guidelines: head-to-head longevity-supplement studies, a new HIIT meta-analysis in middle-aged and older women, pre-surgical pelvic floor training, the AGO 2026 integrative-oncology guideline for breast cancer, and the AASM's latest word on insomnia (plus magnesium). Sources from PubMed, ClinicalTrials.gov, Frontiers, Nature, the AASM, and the AGO are linked as chips under each section. Informational only — discuss anything you'd act on with a clinician.

sections.topic: Anti-Aging — From Mouse Hype to Human Dosing Trials
sections.body:
The field is maturing from splashy animal claims toward **controlled human trials** that measure real aging biomarkers (epigenetic clocks, proteomic "organ age") and pin down safe dosing.

- **Taurine gets its verdict soon.** The **TauAge** RCT (Technical University of Munich, with Stanford & Rutgers; NCT06613542) dosed adults 55–75 with **4 g/day taurine vs. placebo for 6 months**, tracking DNA-methylation age, proteomic organ-age, inflammation (CRP), metabolic markers, and strength. It **completed in November 2025**, so mature human data on whether taurine actually slows biological aging are imminent — a needed reality check after 2023's headline mouse study.
- **Rapamycin dosing, done properly.** The new **RESTOR** early-phase trial (NCT06658093, started **March 2026**) is an adaptive PK/PD study finding the dose/schedule of **rapamycin vs. everolimus** that safely lowers mTOR activity in older adults to "young" levels. Notably, it's powered to detect **sex differences** — investigators expect the optimal dose in women to differ from men. Translation: off-label "longevity" rapamycin is still pre-optimization; dose and timing aren't settled.
- **NMN, head-to-head.** A randomized crossover trial (NCT07144527) is comparing **1,000 mg NMN** against a proprietary NAD⁺ formulation for exercise tolerance and aging biomarkers in adults 60–80 — the kind of active-comparator design the supplement space badly needs.

Practical framing: favor interventions being tested in **RCTs with objective aging biomarkers**, expect **modest** effects, and remember dosing (and sex) may matter as much as the molecule.

sections.body:
A brand-new 2026 meta-analysis sharpens the message for women: **HIIT is a powerful cardio tool, but not a strength tool on its own.**

- **The cardio win is real and robust.** A *Frontiers in Physiology* systematic review & meta-analysis (**19 RCTs**, middle-aged and older women; searched through Nov 2025) found HIIT **significantly raised VO2max** vs. controls (**SMD 1.20**, 95% CI 0.86–1.54) with **high certainty of evidence** — consistent across age, body-mass status, and program length.
- **But it doesn't build strength by itself.** In the same analysis, HIIT did **not** significantly improve **muscle strength** (SMD −0.17), flexibility, or sit-to-stand performance; walking ability improved only borderline (very low certainty). If you want strength and function, HIIT alone won't get you there.
- **So pair it with resistance work.** A randomized trial in women found that combining **HIIT with higher-intensity lower-body resistance training** produced markedly bigger gains in **peak VO2 (+23% vs. +7%)** and **leg strength** than standard moderate-intensity training — with no serious adverse events.

Bottom line: use **2–3 HIIT sessions/week** to drive aerobic fitness, but **add resistance training** for strength, function, and body composition. Progress volume gradually and keep recovery adequate.

sections.body:
**Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT)** stays the evidence-based **first-line** treatment for stress urinary incontinence (SUI). Two fresh 2026 trials show it's powerful enough to change surgical plans — and reaffirm it beats trendier substitutes.

- **PFMT before surgery can defer the surgery.** A randomized trial (*International Urogynecology Journal*, published **March 7, 2026**) put 90 women awaiting mid-urethral sling surgery through **6 weeks of intensive preoperative PFMT** vs. education alone. The training group had large improvements in muscle strength (Modified Oxford, d = 0.85) and symptom severity (d = 0.90) — and in **43% of participants the planned surgery was postponed.** A strong case for structured PFMT as standard pre-surgical care.
- **Pilates isn't a replacement.** A randomized controlled trial in the *Brazilian Journal of Physical Therapy* compared **Mat Pilates** (plus voluntary pelvic-floor contractions) against gold-standard **PFMT** in postmenopausal women with SUI over 3 months. Preliminary results: **PFMT was more effective** — so Pilates may complement, but shouldn't substitute for, targeted training.

Key point: **correct technique and consistency beat sheer reps or novelty.** Confirm you're activating the right muscles (clinician exam or biofeedback), and don't assume a general core/Pilates class replaces dedicated pelvic-floor work.

sections.topic: Alternative & Integrative Options — HER2+ / TP53 Breast Cancer
sections.body:
"Alternative" is best read as **evidence-graded integrative care alongside standard HER2-targeted treatment** — mostly to improve quality of life and tolerability, not to replace therapy. The **AGO 2026** breast-cancer complementary-therapy guideline is a useful map of what has support and what doesn't.

- **What the AGO 2026 guideline actually endorses.** Positive/neutral ("+/−") recommendations go to **exercise** across the care continuum, **acupuncture** and **massage** (symptom/pain relief), **mistletoe** and **ginseng** (reduce fatigue), **L-carnitine** (fatigue, neuropathy), and **ginger** (chemo-induced nausea). It flags **melatonin** as an adjunct (e.g., radiation dermatitis) and repeatedly warns about **CYP3A4 interactions** (ginseng, Ganoderma) with cancer drugs.
- **Mistletoe (Viscum album).** A systematic review & meta-analysis found a **clinically relevant, medium-sized improvement in quality of life** for breast-cancer patients using mistletoe extracts during chemo — likely via immunomodulation — though survival evidence remains unproven.
- **Medicinal mushrooms.** A 2026 *Frontiers* mechanistic review highlights **PSK (Turkey Tail / Trametes versicolor)** and lentinan as immune-supportive adjuncts (NK-cell activity, reduced myelosuppression), with the strongest clinical data in gastric/colorectal and some breast-cancer settings — but calls for better standardized RCTs.
- **Why genetics matter here.** HER2+ tumors carry **TP53 mutations in ~55–75%** of cases, and germline TP53 (Li-Fraumeni) is linked to early-onset HER2+ disease — a reason to coordinate any integrative plan (and supplement timing) closely with your oncology team.

Important framing: use these as **supportive add-ons under clinical supervision** — never as substitutes for HER2-targeted therapy — and always screen for **drug–supplement interactions**.

sections.body:
For chronic, restless, or fragmented sleep, 2026 evidence keeps **behavioral therapy first, pills/supplements second**.

- **CBT-I is still the anchor.** The AASM's 2026 systematic review, meta-analysis, and clinical practice guideline on insomnia reaffirm **cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I)** — sleep restriction, stimulus control, and cognitive restructuring — as first-line, and (echoing the 2017 CPG) recommend **against** relying on **melatonin, valerian, tryptophan, or diphenhydramine** due to insufficient evidence. Medications are best reserved for people who can't do CBT-I or have residual symptoms.
- **Digital CBT-I works in the real world.** A 2026 propensity-matched study of prescription **digital CBT-I (SleepioRx)** found it was associated with **fewer sleep-medication fills** and a sustained drop in outpatient visits — a scalable option when in-person therapy is hard to access.
- **Magnesium — modest, and mostly for the deficient.** A 2025 randomized, placebo-controlled trial (155 adults, poor sleepers) found **250 mg elemental magnesium (bisglycinate) daily for 4 weeks** produced a **small but significant** drop in Insomnia Severity Index (effect size d ≈ 0.2), with benefits concentrated in people with **low baseline dietary magnesium**. Helpful, gentle, but not a cure.

Best-practice habits for restless/disjointed sleep:

1. Keep a **fixed wake time**, even on weekends.
2. Reserve the bed **for sleep only**; keep the room cool, dark, and quiet.
3. Dim lights and cut screens during a wind-down window.
4. If fragmented sleep persists beyond a few weeks, see a provider to **rule out sleep apnea** and consider **CBT-I** (in-person or digital) before medications.
